items.title: National Assembly, Senate pass resolutions endorsing Centre's imposition of emergency in KP
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Shortly after the National Assembly passed a resolution endorsing the federal government’s imposition of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Wednesday, the Senate also gave its approval for the measure. The Centre had imposed governor’s rule and emergency in KP on Sunday, citing the provincial government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the fight against terrorism. Minister for Parliamentary Affairs Tariq Fazal Chaudhry tabled the motions regarding the proclamation of emergency before both Houses. The NA question hour session was suspended due to discussions on the emergency. The motion in the lower House of Parliament was adopted with a majority vote after a discussion opened by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar. “The National Assembly approves the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President on the 11th October, 2026 in the Province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa under second proviso of clause (1) of Article 232 of the Constitution,” read a post by NA’s official X account. According to Article 232 , if the “president acts on his own, the Proclamation of Emergency shall be placed” before both Houses of the Parliament for approval by each House within 10 days. Meanwhile, a proclamation for governor’s rule issued under Article 234 “shall be laid before a joint sitting and shall cease to be in force at the expiration of two months”, unless a joint sitting approves its extension. However, such a measure shall not remain in force for more than six months. Throughout Wednesday’s proceedings, opposition members participated calmly and did not stage any loud protest, unlike past instances of ruckus when PTI objects to the Centre. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also attended part of the session, with pictures released by the NA showing him shaking hands with Opposition Leader Mehmood Khan Achakzai. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif shakes hands with leader of the opposition in the National Assembly, Mehmood Khan Achakzai, on Wednesday. — Photo courtesy NA Facebook Federal ministers defended the emergency imposition while assailing what they described as the PTI-led KP government’s lack of will to combat terrorism. In tune with that, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari blamed the PTI for the circumstances that compelled the Centre to impose emergency in KP and termed it a “political suicide attack” for the party. However, he also urged the treasury and the opposition to get back on the path of dialogue and make joint efforts against terrorism. At one point during the proceedings, NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq noted that the Oct 3 dialogue was held in a cordial atmosphere. Sadiq praised both sides for “attempting more than their capacity so that the matter is settled”. However, he said some matters were beyond the parties’ control and voiced his support for forming the same committees for negotiations if ever needed in the future. Addressing PTI lawmakers, the speaker said, “Everyone’s response was that this [process of dialogue] should continue, but you also understand that your hands were tied.” He took note of the PTI’s complaints regarding the jail conditions of party founder Imran Khan, adding that he had even provided details of facilities provided to the jailed ex-premier. The session was adjourned to meet again at 11am on Oct 16 (Friday). ‘Political suicide attack’ Bilawal began his speech by highlighting that emergency and governor’s rule in KP were measures taken under the Constitution . Reading the relevant provisions, he asserted that the Centre tried its best to “engage the opposition so this step did not have to be taken”. “They will have to accept, even if not publicly, but the responsible leadership of the opposition knows that the PTI itself carried out a political suicide attack on its KP government,” he remarked. The PPP chief maintained that the PTI could not deny that its “leadership, particularly in the province had a key role in the political, constitutional and legal circumstances” at present. Bilawal emphasised that the PPP’s stance was that “before employing this constitutional atomic bomb, we must engage with PTI and the opposition and try to address the federal government’s reservations that they were not supporting them in the war against terrorism”. He observed: “If political space is restricted for one political party, it is impossible that it remains restricted for that particular party; it is limited for every political party, political worker and Pakistani citizen. “We are responsible for this, but you cannot deny that you are also responsible for it,” he said. Terming the imposition of emergency a “difficult decision”, Bilawal recalled alleged remarks by Sohail Afridi — the KP chief minister whose role is now non-functional — that he would not combat terrorism the way the Centre wanted. “If this was not a political suicide, then what else was it?” The Bhutto scion wondered if the opposition and Afridi had left any reason for President Asif Ali Zardari, who he said prides himself on passing the 18th Amendment, to “refuse to sign” the emergency proclamation. He argued that due to the PTI’s actions and statements, neither the president, the Centre, nor he had any legal or political reason left for not imposing emergency in KP. “But even today, I would recommend to the federal government that we extend our hand forward once again for negotiations, political discussions and try to find a resolution and a middle path,” Bilawal added. The PPP chairman noted that emergency was “always a stopgap measure”. “We cannot sustain the emergency forever,” he added, emphasising that while the counterterrorism fight would be better than before, an “all-of-society and all-of-country response” was needed to eradicate it completely. Regarding the Oct 3 talks of a joint delegation of the PPP and the government with the opposition, Bilawal said, “Late at night, I was informed that congratulations, negotiations are succeeding.” He said the PTI was willing to declare the areas in KP with surging terrorism as “terrorist areas”, and the opposition was about to agree that the federal and KP governments would sign a pact on joint efforts against terrorism. However, the dialogue collapsed. The former foreign minister pointed out that the security challenges Pakistan was facing were “way more complicated” than before, adding that India “could still not digest […] its embarrassment” from the May 2025 conflict . Referring to remarks by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi that its ‘ Operation Sindoor ’ was still ongoing, Bilawal said: “It means that India is still sponsoring terrorist incidents in Pakistan, sometimes in the form of TTP (Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan) and sometimes in the form of separatist terrorist groups.” He reiterated Pakistan’s stance that India was involved in terrorist activities being conducted from across the Afghan border. The ex-foreign minister then highlighted Islamabad’s role as a mediator in the US-Iran war. “But there is a state — which we do not recognise as a state — that will neither be happy nor ever forget that you took this step. And those Zionist forces will and are interfering in Pakistan’s internal politics and state.” Concluding his speech, the PPP chairman emphasised the need for building consensus on “some fundamental issues” for an empowered lower house. “Even today, we are saying, come and at least begin from this house,” he said while addressing the opposition benches. Gohar demands implementation of NAP Speaking on the NA floor, PTI Chairman Gohar Ali Khan’s said his party “rejected” the Centre’s move to impose emergency in KP. He asked what “terrorism” Imran’s wife or sisters had allegedly been involved in that they had been put behind bars, or what the accusations were against the PTI MNAs and MPAs who he said were detained. Gohar further said, “One person is not present in the house currently. When he comes during a joint session, then I will reveal the reality of the negotiations.” He affirmed that the PTI had raised its voice against terrorism, adding that measures against the scourge must be taken according to the National Action Plan (NAP). Gohar argued that the PML-N opposition during the PTI’s tenure carried out “14 long marches in two years, but you did not let us stage even one long march”. Presenting his version of the Oct 3 talks with the government, the PTI leader said his party was being asked to immediately call off the long march . “I said where did [the topic] of terrorism arise from suddenly.” Noting that the government had put forward “five reservations”, Gohar said PTI was willing to make the KP Police Act similar to that of Punjab and Sindh. The PTI leader reiterated his party’s request for the production of certain MNAs it says were taken into custody. Gohar also welcomed Bilawal’s proposal to continue dialogue. Responding to Gohar’s remarks, the PPP chairman said the PTI was busy in its long march while the people of KP were being targeted by terrorists. Bilawal reiterated that the opposition could keep arguing against the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP, but no one could deny that the decision was grounded in the Constitution. “I cannot insist on the government to continue talks with PTI despite being defrauded multiple times,” the PPP chairman said. Pointing towards Gohar and Achakzai, Bilawal said: “I believe that none of them is allied with terrorists. I believe that they will definitely want to combat terrorism; however, they cannot deny the fact that their former chief minister contradicted this fact.” Bilawal again requested all the stakeholders to unite and combat terrorism collectively. He also called for the provision of all facilities to the incarcerated PTI founder. ‘Threat to national security’ Addressing the house, the law minister explained that emergency was imposed in KP as the security situation there was becoming a threat to “national security”. Tarar noted that after the Proclamation of Emergency was issued, the Constitution’s Article 232 required that both houses of the parliament approve the measure. He recalled that the federal cabinet examined “material” regarding terrorism in the province during its Oct 11 meeting and then advised PM Shehbaz to recommend the imposition of emergency. He noted that some people compared the measure to the emergency imposed by former dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf on Oct 12, 1999. The minister particularly noted “internal disturbances” and cross-border infiltrations. He contended that the situation since Oct 15, 2025, when Sohail Afridi’s government came into power in KP , was “turning into a threat to national security to an alarming extent”. He went on to highlight that there was a rise in terrorism in KP, especially after 2021, due to the approach of the provincial government. “Perhaps there might be foreign, diplomatic and political reasons behind it, which got inflamed due to a political party’s point of view.” Tarar stated that 2,911 incidents of terrorism took place between 2021 and 2024 in KP, but they surged to 3,787 incidents between Oct 15, 2025 and Oct 9, 2026. He criticised the KP chief minister for ignoring martyred security and police personnel, and for instead preferring to promote his political designs and make visits across the country. “Even this was announced that the federal capital will be conquered,” he said, referring to the party’s plan to hold a protest long march towards the federal capital. The PML-N leader expressed his government’s gratitude to NA Speaker Ayaz Sadiq for providing a platform for dialogue between the Centre and the opposition. He reiterated the government’s stance that the PTI had the agreement draft changed multiple times, but even then backed off from it. Tarar observed that the PTI demanded the release of their party founder Imran Khan and his treatment in a private hospital despite knowing that only courts could provide such a relief. He said two days would be “remembered in the country’s democratic history with regard to misfortune and a political party”. On the emergency measure, the law minister noted that a special mechanism has been introduced for 12 districts of KP. Speaking after Tarar, Achakzai criticised him for trying to prove that terrorism was not tackled in KP. The opposition leader questioned the government’s mandate in the February 2024 general elections, quipping that the opposition would “surrender” if the minister could swear that the government won those polls fairly. Achakzai alleged that the incumbent ruling coalition was formed “illegally”. ‘You do not have clean hands’ Meanwhile, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif went on to recall the tenure of the PTI government in the Centre and assailed the party’s past actions. Referring to ex-prime minister Imran Khan’s plan to resettle members of the TTP, he said PTI tried to convince the then-opposition that “bringing these terrorists back would be better for Pakistan”. The PML-N leader mentioned the 2019 episode of an Indian pilot’s capture in Pakistan: “They had threatened and we were surrendering. The then-prime minister was saying, ‘What should I do? Attack India?’” Asif urged the opposition to reflect on its past actions, adding that Imran often used to praise former army chief retired General Qamar Javed Bajwa. “As long as this contradiction remains in our words and actions and in our society, the circumstances of this country will not fix.” He narrated his time behind bars during the PTI government, when Shehbaz “smuggled a blanket” to him to brace the low temperatures. “I used to eat the jail’s food,” he said, claiming that orders were given to remove the geyser when it was installed. “But we did not hold rallies or mourn at D-Chowk or dig graves. We did not martyr police and law enforcement personnel,” Asif remarked. “You demand equity when you have clean hands. You do not have clean hands, you cannot demand equity; this is a thousand-year-old principle,” he contended. “You know very well what Gen Musharraf did to me. There was a 4x6 cell in Attock jail,” the PML-N politician said, emphasising that he stood with his party and ex-PM Nawaz Sharif. Speaking on the current political situation, Asif alleged that Afridi used to “take directives […] from a person sitting in Afghanistan”. He referred to a statement by the TTP condemning the imposition of emergency and deployment of troops in certain places. “Who is their ally and who is their rival?” he said. The minister further countered the PTI’s stance that its leaders have not been able to meet Imran, who is imprisoned in the Adiala jail. “Meetings are held, [but] a lot of them are not publicised or brought on record,” he maintained. Farooq Sattar urges PTI to ‘openly condemn terrorism’ In his remarks on the floor of the lower house, Farooq Sattar expressed Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan’s (MQM-P) confidence in the decision taken by the prime minister. “This was an extremely difficult decision, but so unavoidable that you had no other option,” Sattar said about imposing emergency and governor’s rule. “We trust your decision as we trust your experience, capabilities, political acumen, and that you made this decision in the interest of the nation,” he added. The MQM-P lawmaker contended that the PTI was “on the wrong side and does not have concrete arguments” to declare that the decision was baseless or made with political motives. “The main issue is of the mindset,” he declared, adding that Imran had “publicly said that the war on terror is not ours”. “This is their policy. This is their mindset.” Sattar questioned whether the KP government had ever published reports to expose terrorist hideouts and extremist trends. He further raised questions about the government’s pursuit of cases against suspected terrorists. “Openly condemn terrorism; else, the allegation of backing [it], if a commission is formed and God forbid, it is proven in the inquiry that there is political extremism and terrorism complicity, there is a nexus, then where will you go?” Sattar recounted his past MQM experiences, saying, “I have also suffered such times. A lot of times, the narrative coming from the top was difficult to defend. Today, I feel that Barrister Gohar is also not in the position to defend his [party’s] position on KP.”

items.title: Niger : la France expulse un officier paraplégique qui a combattu à ses côtés, Niamey dénonce «l’ingratitude»
items.description: Le ministre nigerien de la Justice et des Droits de l'homme Alio Daouda a vivement denonce, le 13 octobre, l'expulsion de deux agents de l'ambassade du Niger a Paris. Dans une declaration diffusee par la television publique nigerienne, il a qualifie la decision francaise d'« acte d'ingratitude grave et inacceptable ». Blesse aux cotes des Francais, expulse avec sa famille L'un des agents nigeriens expulses par la France avait participe a des combats au Niger dans le cadre d'une operation menee par Paris. Le ministre a particulierement insiste sur le cas de cet homme, Abdoul-Razak Ibrahim Moussa Toro. Le 30 juillet 2014, il participait a une mission dans la region de Diffa, au sud-est du Niger. Grievement atteint a la colonne vertebrale, il est devenu paraplegique. Il avait alors ete evacue en France pour etre soigne. Douze ans plus tard, Paris exigeait son depart. « Peut-on chasser un homme blesse, mutile et rendu inapte au service d'une cooperation que l'on a soi-meme voulue, ordonnee et payee ? », s'est indigne le ministre. Aujourd'hui, l'expulsion d'un ancien partenaire militaire, blesse lors d'une mission commune, est devenue pour Niamey le symbole du traitement reserve par Paris a ceux qui l'ont servie. Le ministre l'a resume sans detour : « Voila comment la France remercie ceux qui ont servi a ses cotes. Elle sollicite les hommes, elle les engage et les finance. Puis lorsqu'ils tombent, elle les met a la porte avec leur famille quitte a devancer ses propres tribunaux. » Les deux agents avaient ete declares persona non grata le 16 septembre. Trois jours plus tard, ils quittaient la France. Pour l'un d'eux, ce depart force s'est fait en famille, enfants compris, malgre une procedure engagee devant la justice. Le 25 septembre, soit six jours apres leur depart, le tribunal administratif de Versailles a annule l'obligation de quitter le territoire francais qui lui avait ete delivree, a precise le ministre. « Peut-on invoquer partout les droits de l'homme et l'etat de droit, puis expulser un homme pour echapper au jugement de ses propres juges ? », a-t-il demande. Le Quai d'Orsay n'a pas commente l'affaire. La rupture entre Paris et Niamey se creuse Les relations entre les deux pays se sont profondement degradees depuis 2023. Niamey a denonce les accords militaires conclus avec l'ancienne puissance coloniale et obtenu le depart des soldats francais . En decembre de la meme annee, Paris fermait son ambassade au Niger , tandis que celle du Niger restait ouverte en France. Les griefs se sont accumules depuis. Dans la nuit du 28 au 29 août, une mutinerie a eclate autour de la base 101 et de plusieurs sites strategiques de Niamey, avant d'etre progressivement contenue par les forces nigeriennes et leurs allies. Le pouvoir d'Emmanuel Macron a ete accuse de l'avoir soutenue.

items.title: 2027: Build your own results machinery or don’t contest – Agbakoba tells parties
items.description: Senior Advocate of Nigeria, Dr. Olisa Agbakoba, has told political parties that those unable to collect and preserve their own election results have no business on the ballot, warning that they cannot lean on the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to prove their case in court. Speaking on ARISE NEWS on Wednesday, Agbakoba said parties that want to challenge INEC’s declarations in 2027 must be ready to present authenticated results of their own, gathered through agents deployed across polling units. “If you’re not ready to monitor the elections right across Nigeria, don’t go on the ballot. Or don’t complain,” he said. He criticised the common practice of parties heading to court to ask judges to compel INEC to release results from its Result Viewing Portal (IReV), describing it as “lazy.” In his view, party agents already sign the polling unit result sheets (Form EC8A) and should hold those records themselves. Agbakoba explained that INEC is presumed to have acted regularly in official matters, a presumption parties can only overcome with credible evidence. A party that shows up in court with its own verified records, he said, puts the court in a position to see “something else that is coming from the same source,” which can rebut that presumption. A party without such records, he added, has “no reason to question” it. The senior lawyer noted that this approach has never been tested in earlier presidential election petitions, but said he hopes it will change in 2027. He predicted that parties would use AI tools to pull results from IReV and produce faster tallies, and that such parallel compilations could pressure INEC to be more accurate because it would know it was being watched. On the right to publish results, Agbakoba cited the 1984 case of NUJ v. FEDECO (INEC’s predecessor), saying it affirmed that anyone may publish results already in the public domain. INEC’s exclusive power, he said, is only to declare a winner. He added that the Electoral Act itself penalises publishing fake results, which implies that publishing genuine ones is allowed. For media houses using AI to collate and project outcomes, he set one condition: results must come from IReV and be clearly attributed to it. The post 2027: Build your own results machinery or don’t contest – Agbakoba tells parties appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le Burkina Faso et les Pays-Bas échangent pour le renforcement de la coopération au développement
items.description: Le Camarade ministre des Affaires étrangères, Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE accompagné de la Camarade ministre déléguée, Bêbgnasgnan Stella Eldine KABRE/KABORE, a accordé une audience au Directeur du développement social au ministère des Affaires étrangères des Pays-Bas, Monsieur Peter-Dereck HOF accompagné par la Chargée d’affaires de l’ambassade des Pays-Bas, Dr Margret VERWIJIK. A sa sortie d’audience, Monsieur Peter-Dereck HOF a indiqué qu’il s’agit de sa première visite au Burkina Faso, qui vise à mieux prendre connaissance du contexte national, afin de se faire sa propre opinion sur la gestion actuelle du pays et sur les perspectives de la coopération au développement entre les Pays-Bas et le Burkina Faso. Il est aussi question pour l’émissaire néerlandais d’écouter les autorités burkinabè sur les priorités nationales, avec pour objectif de mieux réorienter les interventions des Pays-Bas au Burkina Faso. Le Directeur du développement social au ministère des Affaires étrangères des Pays-Bas, Peter-Dereck Hof Saluant cette visite du Directeur du développement social du ministère des Affaires étrangères des Pays-Bas, le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè lui a présenté le contexte qui prévalait au Burkina Faso avant l’avènement du régime en place, ainsi que les réformes mises en place ayant permis des résultats dans plusieurs secteurs tels que la sécurité, l’humanitaire, la santé, l’éducation et les infrastructures. Sur la politique étrangère du Burkina Faso, le Camarade Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE a indiqué que celle-ci est axée sur l’affirmation de la souveraineté, la diversification des partenariats, sans oublier que désormais notre pays est maitre de la définition des programmes et des mécanismes de leur suivi et évaluation, les partenaires étant invités à s’aligner sur les priorités du gouvernement. Il a par ailleurs reconnu la nécessité de renforcer la coopération au développement avec les partenaires dans une approche de proximité et de dialogue, tout en saluant les Pays-Bas qui reste engagés auprès du Burkina Faso pour ce type de partenariat. Le séjour du diplomate néerlandais a commencé par une visite d’un projet de pisciculture au barrage de Ziga, soutenu par une ONG néerlandaise et visant à accompagner l’autonomisation économique des femmes. La coopération entre le Burkina Faso et les Pays-Bas, date de plus de 6 décennies et portent sur les secteurs comme la santé, l'agriculture et la gestion de l'eau, l'éducation, l'entrepreneuriat des jeunes et de l’autonomisation économique des femmes. DCRP/MAE NB: le titre est de la rédaction L’article Le Burkina Faso et les Pays-Bas échangent pour le renforcement de la coopération au développement est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: FCC rejects Bushra Bibi's petition seeking suspension of 7-year Al-Qadir Trust sentence
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) on Wednesday rejected a plea moved by the spouse of incarcerated former prime minister Imran Khan, Bushra Bibi, seeking suspension of her seven-year sentence in the £190 Al-Qadir Trust case . “We find no sufficient ground warranting interference with the April 30 Islamabad High Court (IHC) order at this stage,” FCC Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan observed, who headed the two-judge bench that rejected Bushra Bibi’s plea. The IHC has declined to dismiss her plea for the suspension of her sentence as an appeal against her and Imran’s conviction remained pending before the high court. The FCC bench, which included Justice Ali Baqar Najafi, expressed the expectation that the high court would endeavour to decide the main appeal against her conviction, affording both sides adequate opportunity of hearing while discouraging unnecessary adjournments. Earlier in the day, the bench had reserved its ruling on the plea, which contended that Bushra Bibi, being a woman and in view of her serious medical condition, was entitled to the suspension of her sentence, as similar relief was contemplated under the first proviso to Section 497(1), CrPC, which deals with cases where bail may be granted in ease of a non-bailable offence. In its three-page order, the FCC noted that the application seeking the suspension of the sentence had remained pending before the IHC on account of successive adjournments sought by the National Accountability Bureau (NAB). It observed that, without entering into the merits of the application under Section 426 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the IHC had declined to suspend the sentence principally on the ground that the main appeal had already been fixed for hearing and the appellant’s counsel was not extending the requisite assistance towards its adjudication. The record further reflected that the appeal, initially fixed for April 30, was subsequently adjourned to May 7 and thereafter to Oct 5. The principal grievance urged by the counsel for the appellant pertained to the repeated adjournments allegedly sought by NAB, resulting in the prolongation of proceedings on the application for the suspension of her sentence, the FCC observed. “Be that as it may, the main appeal having already been fixed for hearing, the appropriate course will be to secure its expeditious adjudication rather than undertake a parallel examination of the merits of the suspension of sentence at this stage,” the FCC stated. The FCC order further said that the appellant’s assertion that the appeal involved a voluminous record necessitating elaborate arguments did not, by itself, furnished a sufficient justification for interference with the IHC order. It was, therefore, incumbent upon the appellant’s counsel to extend full assistance to the IHC in hearing the main appeal, following which NAB would be equally obligated to advance its arguments without unnecessary adjournments, the FCC declared. The FCC also noted that the criminal appeal before it was barred by 61 days, for which the appellant had sought condonation of delay. The explanation furnished, particularly the appellant’s incarceration at the Adiala jail, constituted sufficient cause warranting the condonation, the FCC observed while condoning the delay. The appeal Moved under Section 32-A of the National Accountability Ordinance read with Article 175F(1)(a) of the Constitution, the criminal appeal pleaded before the FCC that, despite earlier directions issued by the IHC to the authorities of Central Jail Adiala to facilitate a meeting between the appellant and her counsel, the jail authorities were not complying with the directions. Her counsel was instead permitted to meet the appellant’s husband, Imran Khan, who disclosed that both he and the appellant were being illegally kept in solitary confinement. They were allegedly denied access to family, friends, counsel and political party members, as well as to each other, and were not provided with books or television, thereby subjecting them to complete isolation from human contact and depriving them of information about the outside world. The same was subsequently confirmed by the appellant’s daughters upon meeting her after her eye surgery on April 17, the appeal stated. Such treatment amounted to an unauthorised enhancement of sentence, violated the prisoners’ fundamental rights to life and dignity guaranteed under Article 9 of the Constitution, and warranted immediate intervention by the FCC, the petition argued. The appeal stated that the appellant had been subjected to continuous solitary confinement, which had demonstrably taken a grave toll on her physical and mental health. This was evident from the fact that she had to be taken outside the jail premises for eye surgery. In view of her deteriorating medical condition, she ought not to be subjected to solitary confinement even if such punishment had been awarded by a court. However, in blatant disregard of the applicable law and prison rules, she continued to be subjected to such unlawful confinement, the petition pleaded. The appeal contended that NAB had selectively prosecuted the appellant and her husband while deliberately excluding six other individuals who were allegedly implicated in the matter. The core allegations revolved around the Malik Riaz family and other persons who had conspicuously not been subjected to prosecution. This selective and incomplete approach had resulted in a defective and biased investigation, culminating in the unjust framing of charges and subsequent conviction of the appellant, the appeal contended. Thus, the prosecution had failed to present cogent, reliable and legally admissible evidence to substantiate the allegations in their entirety. The former first lady was handed the sentence in the case in January last year, and remains imprisoned at Rawalpindi’s Adiala jail. In the case, the court had found Imran and Bushra guilty of giving undue favours to property tycoon Riaz in retrieving his laundered money from the United Kingdom. Bushra, along with the ex-PM, had initially moved the IHC for the suspension of her sentence in July last year. But the high court dismissed their requests in May 2026, observing that their appeals against their convictions had already been fixed for hearing. Subsequently, the two approached the Supreme Court (SC) against the IHC decision, but the SC office returned the petition as being not maintainable, explaining that since the IHC had passed the impugned order while exercising jurisdiction under Section 32 of the National Accountability Ordinance (NAO), 1999, the remedy lay exclusively before the FCC under Section 32-A of the ordinance. Bushra then moved the FCC on July 30, with her criminal appeal contending that the appellant, being a woman with a serious medical condition, was entitled to the suspension of her sentence, as similar relief was contemplated under the first proviso to Section 497(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC). Earlier this month, senior members of the PTI’s legal team approached the FCC for early fixation of the criminal appeal. However, no fresh application was filed, and only a verbal request was made for early registration and fixation of the case. Her latest application for the appeal’s early hearing, which was rejected on Monday, also stated that her rapidly deteriorating ocular condition threatened her remaining eyesight.

Public money belongs to the people, not government officials – Ato Forson
items.description: Finance Minister Dr. Cassiel Ato Forson has called on public officials to account for every cedi entrusted to them and build systems that make the recovery of public money an exception rather than an annual ritual. He was speaking at an engagement on the Auditor-General’s Report attended by regional ministers and metropolitan, municipal and district chief executives. Dr. Forson stressed that government officials are custodians of the nation’s resources, not their owners, and must manage those resources with a clear sense of responsibility to citizens. “Public money does not belong to government officials, we are only the custodians of those resources,” he said. “Those resources belong to the people of Ghana: Our constituents, our citizens!” He urged officials to reclaim every recoverable cedi, underscoring their obligation to account for the public funds placed in their care. “So let us recover every cedi, that is recoverable! Let us account for every cedi that is entrusted to us as public officials,” he stated. The Finance Minister, however, made clear that accountability must go beyond recovering money. He called for stronger systems to protect public resources, rather than allowing recovery to become a recurring feature of public financial management. “But above all, let us build systems where recovery becomes the exception, not an annual ritual,” he said.

items.title: Power, politics and the battle for electoral credibility: Is Ghana’s electoral commission truly independent?
items.description: Nothing tests the strength of a democracy quite like an election. Elections ignite hopes, heighten anxieties, expose political rivalries and sometimes deepen national divisions. Beyond determining who governs, they provide a peaceful mechanism for resolving political competition and confer legitimacy on those entrusted with public power. But what happens when the very institution responsible for safeguarding the people’s mandate becomes the subject of political suspicion? That is the uncomfortable question confronting Ghana as the controversy surrounding the appointment of two Deputy Electoral Commissioners by President John Dramani Mahama reignites debate about the independence, credibility and impartiality of the Electoral Commission (EC). Why is the New Patriotic Party (NPP) so concerned about the appointments? Is its opposition rooted in legitimate institutional concerns, partisan calculations, or a mixture of both? And, more fundamentally, what do these political battles reveal about the independence of Ghana’s electoral management body? These are questions that deserve more than partisan talking points. They demand a closer examination of the constitutional framework, the history of appointments to the Commission and the political circumstances that have shaped public perceptions of its neutrality. THE INDEPENDENCE QUESTION: WHAT DOES THE CONSTITUTION REALLY GUARANTEE? Ghana’s 1992 Constitution establishes the Electoral Commission as an independent constitutional body entrusted with responsibilities central to the country’s democratic survival. Article 45 outlines the Commission’s functions, including the compilation of the voters’ register, the conduct and supervision of public elections and referenda, and voter education in collaboration with the National Commission for Civic Education (NCCE). Article 43 provides for the composition of the Commission, while Article 46 expressly guarantees its independence by stipulating that, in the performance of its functions, the Commission shall not be subject to the direction or control of any person or authority. On paper, the constitutional safeguards are clear. The EC is expected to operate independently, free from political interference and undue influence. Yet constitutional guarantees and institutional realities are not always the same. Article 70 gives the President a central role in appointing the Chairperson, Deputy Chairpersons and other members of the Commission, acting in consultation with the Council of State. Article 195 also establishes the President’s role in public-service appointments, subject to the constitutional provisions governing the relevant offices. This arrangement raises an important institutional question: Can an electoral management body be perceived as completely independent when the President, who is also the leader of a political administration, plays a decisive role in appointing its top officials? The question is not whether presidential appointment automatically makes an Electoral Commissioner partisan. It does not. Rather, the issue is whether the appointment process provides sufficient safeguards to inspire confidence across the political spectrum. The absence of a parliamentary confirmation process for these appointments, for instance, limits the extent to which nominees are subjected to public scrutiny through a formal legislative vetting process. Questions also arise about the Commission’s financial autonomy, administrative arrangements and the procedures governing appointments within the institution. CHARLOTTE OSEI’S EXIT: THE CONTROVERSY THAT REFUSES TO DISAPPEAR To understand the current debate, Ghana must revisit one of the most contentious episodes in the recent history of its Electoral Commission: the removal of Charlotte Osei and her two deputies in 2018. Appointed in June 2015 under President John Dramani Mahama, Osei became the first woman to serve as Chairperson of Ghana’s Electoral Commission. Her tenure, however, was marked by tensions and controversy that culminated in her removal in June 2018 under President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo. The removals followed an investigation initiated through a committee constituted under the authority of the then Chief Justice, Sophia Akuffo, after allegations of misconduct were raised against the Commission’s leadership. The officials were removed following the constitutionally prescribed process. Nevertheless, the episode left a lasting political and institutional legacy. For critics of the process, the circumstances surrounding the removal intensified concerns about the vulnerability of the Commission’s leadership to political developments at the highest levels of government. For others, the constitutional procedure demonstrated that even senior electoral officials were not beyond accountability. The controversy became even more politically charged because the NPP, then in government, had previously been a vocal critic of Osei’s leadership while in opposition and profess her removal if they won the 2016 election. That history inevitably raises a difficult question: Did the change in the Commission’s leadership strengthen public confidence in its independence, or did it deepen suspicions that the institution’s leadership could become entangled in partisan power struggles? The answer cannot be established by political rhetoric alone. It requires evidence, institutional analysis and a careful assessment of the Commission’s conduct before, during and after elections. FROM ONE LEADERSHIP TO ANOTHER: HAS THE TRUST DEFICIT BEEN RESOLVED? Following the 2018 removals, President Akufo-Addo nominated Jean Adukwei Mensa as Electoral Commission Chairperson, alongside Samuel Tettey and Eric Bossman as Deputy Commissioners, and Adwoa Asuama Abrefa as another member. The new leadership was sworn into office on 1 August 2018. The appointments marked a new chapter in the Commission’s history, but they did not end the broader debate about presidential influence over electoral administration. The real test of an Electoral Commission is not simply the political identity of the appointing authority or the public reputation of its appointees. It is whether the institution consistently demonstrates impartiality, transparency, procedural fairness and accountability. An electoral management body may act lawfully and still struggle to convince a section of the public that it is impartial. Equally, political accusations against the body do not, by themselves, establish that it has acted improperly. This distinction is crucial. In a highly competitive multiparty system such as Ghana’s, electoral decisions are routinely scrutinised through partisan lenses. An appointment that one party regards as administratively sound may be interpreted by another as politically consequential. That is precisely why the appointment process must be sufficiently transparent to withstand suspicion, scrutiny and political disagreement. THE TWO DEPUTY COMMISSIONERS: WHY THE POLITICAL TEMPERATURE? The controversy surrounding the appointment of two Deputy Electoral Commissioners by President Mahama on Monday, October 12, 2026 raises a broader question about how Ghana manages the relationship between constitutional authority and public confidence. W Why is the NPP raising concerns about the appointments of Emelia Affi Agbenyo and Joseph Kwaku Asamoah, PhD? What specific constitutional, procedural or substantive objections has the party advanced? Does it challenge the qualifications of the nominees, the appointment process, the potential implications for electoral administration, or the broader institutional arrangement? These questions must be answered against the documented statements and the actual circumstances of the appointments. The NPP’s position should not automatically be dismissed as partisan obstruction. Equally, its objections should not be accepted uncritically merely because they are presented as a defense of electoral independence. A credible analysis must apply the same standard to every political party, whether in government or opposition. If the party believes the appointments threaten the Commission’s neutrality, it must explain precisely how. If its concerns relate to the absence of adequate consultation, transparency or institutional safeguards, those arguments deserve serious public examination. But if the objections are inconsistent with the party’s previous positions on presidential appointment powers, that inconsistency also deserves scrutiny. The central issue is not simply who gets appointed. It is whether the process protects the Electoral Commission from partisan capture and gives Ghanaians compelling reasons to trust its decisions. That is a national democratic concern, not the exclusive property of any political party. BEYOND PARTISAN POLITICS: FOUR TESTS OF ELECTORAL INDEPENDENCE The independence of the EC should be assessed against clear institutional criteria rather than the changing political interests of the parties. First: Appointment and tenure. Are the procedures for appointing and removing commissioners sufficiently transparent and protected against arbitrary political influence? Do they inspire confidence among competing political parties and the wider public? Second: Financial and administrative autonomy. Does the Commission have adequate control over the resources and administrative arrangements necessary to carry out its constitutional mandate without undue external pressure? Third: Operational impartiality. Does the EC apply electoral laws, regulations and procedures consistently, irrespective of which party stands to benefit? Are its decisions explained clearly and communicated in a timely manner? Fourth: Transparency and accountability. Does the Commission provide sufficient information to enable citizens, political parties, civil society organisations and independent observers to scrutinise its decisions? Are complaints handled fairly and through credible procedures? These four tests provide a more meaningful framework for examining electoral independence than the political affiliations or perceived loyalties of individual commissioners. They also provide a basis for assessing the Commission’s performance across elections, including the conduct of the 2020 polls. Any claim that the EC favoured or disadvantaged a particular party must be supported by verifiable evidence, documented decisions and a defensible analysis of its actions. Suspicion alone cannot substitute for proof. WHY PUBLIC CONFIDENCE MATTERS The implications of this debate extend far beyond the appointment of Emelia Affi Agbenyo and Joseph Kwaku Asamoah, PhD. The Electoral Commission of Ghana as it is in other civilised democracies derive much of their authority from public confidence in their impartiality. Their decisions must be respected not because they are immune from criticism, but because the institutions making those decisions are seen to operate according to fair and predictable rules. When confidence deteriorates, even routine administrative decisions can become flashpoints for political confrontation. Voter registration, ballot administration, results collation and the declaration of winners may all attract heightened suspicion. The danger is that persistent distrust can weaken the perceived legitimacy of electoral outcomes, regardless of whether particular decisions are legally defensible. THE BIGGER QUESTION: WHO PROTECTS THE ELECTORAL COMMISSION FROM POLITICS? Ultimately, the controversy over the appointment of the two Deputy Electoral Commissioners exposes a constitutional and democratic dilemma that Ghana has yet to resolve fully. The Constitution guarantees the EC’s independence, but the process through which its leadership is appointed leaves room for continuing debate about the relationship between executive authority and electoral autonomy. The answer is not necessarily to declare every presidential appointment illegitimate. Nor is it to dismiss every objection as political mischief. Rather, Ghana must confront the institutional weaknesses and perceptions that allow electoral appointments to become recurring sources of partisan conflict. Reforms could include greater transparency in the nomination process, clearly articulated and publicly accessible qualification criteria, stronger safeguards for tenure, and a more open framework for scrutinising nominees. Any proposed reform must be carefully designed to preserve the Commission’s independence rather than transfer political influence from one institution to another. The ultimate objective should be to ensure that commissioners command confidence because of their competence, integrity and demonstrable impartiality—not merely because a particular government appointed them. CONCLUSION: A TEST FOR GHANA’S DEMOCRACY The NPP’s opposition to the two Deputy Commissioner appointments presents an opportunity to confront a question that transcends party politics: is Ghana doing enough to insulate its Electoral Commission from political influence and protect public confidence in its work? The party must substantiate its objections. The government must demonstrate that the appointment process is constitutionally sound and institutionally defensible. The Electoral Commission must continue to uphold transparency, impartiality and accountability. Above all, Ghanaians must insist that electoral institutions serve the Republic rather than the interests of the political parties that compete to govern it. Because, in the final analysis, the credibility of an election is determined not only by the ballots cast or the results declared, but also by whether citizens have compelling reasons to believe that the institution overseeing the process has acted fairly. The real battle, therefore, is bigger than two appointments. It is a battle for public trust, institutional independence and the future credibility of Ghana’s democracy.

items.title: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia 'totally unacceptable', says Dar
items.description: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday said that Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia were “totally unacceptable”. He made the remarks while addressing a joint press conference alongside Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, who is currently on an official visit to Pakistan, following the eighth session of the Pakistan-Oman Joint Ministerial Commission (JMC). At the outset of the press conference, Dar said that the two sides would sign a protocol relating to the commission. He said that this reflected “a shared resolve to further strengthen and expand bilateral cooperation in areas of mutual interest”. He said that the two sides would also sign an agreement for mutual visa exemption for holders of diplomatic and official passports. “Pakistan-Oman friendship remains strong and forward-looking,” he told the media. The two ministers would also sign “a number of bilateral agreements” later in the day, Dar said. He added that the two ministers had also agreed to hold a business-to-business investment forum in Pakistan. The ministers discussed the situation in the Gulf as well, he said, adding that “Pakistan remained committed to contributing constructively to diplomatic efforts aimed at promoting peace and stability in the region”. Dar said that the two sides also exchanged views on recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. He said that he conveyed Pakistan’s condemnation of the attacks. “I underscored that attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure are totally unacceptable. My brother [Albusaidi] actually fully endorses this. Violations of international law pose a serious threat to regional peace and security,” he said. “I reaffirmed Pakistan’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and our unwavering commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security in accordance with the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” he said. They also “emphasised the urgent need for unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance to the people of Gaza”, Dar said. DPM Dar also stressed that India’s unilateral abeyance of the Indus Water Treaty was “a material breach of international law”. “This action threatens the water, food and energy security of Pakistan’s 250 million people,” Dar said. Speaking at the occasion, Albusaidi said the JMC had “provided an important opportunity to review the state of bilateral relations”. He said that two sides “reaffirmed the strength of the longstanding ties” between the two countries. “Both Oman and Pakistan attach great importance to dialogue and diplomacy as essential means of addressing regional challenges, easing tensions and promoting peace and stability,” Albusaidi said. He also appreciated Pakistan’s diplomatic role in the US-Iran war . He reaffirmed the two countries’ “shared commitment to further deepening our bilateral partnership and broadening cooperation across centres of mutual benefit”. The two countries agreed that dialogue and diplomacy were “the only way forward” to resolve regional conflicts, Dar said in response to a reporter’s question. “We are both on the same page,” he said. Meanwhile, Dar told reporters that a free trade agreement between Pakistan and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) would help expand business activities, adding that he was told that barring one, all countries had consented to the agreement. Responding to a question about the gaps in bilateral talks between the two countries, Dar said Albusaidi’s visit was previously delayed because Pakistan had been involved in mediation efforts between the US and Iran. Albusaidi added that discussions had continued “behind the scenes”. Responding to a question about the Strait of Hormuz, Albusaidi said that Oman was committed to “unhindered navigation” through the strait “because of its vitality to the global economy and the region”. JMC session The meeting of the commission was co-chaired by Dar and Albusaidi. The two sides “reaffirmed their close fraternal ties and commitment to expanding bilateral cooperation, particularly in trade and investment, maritime and logistics connectivity, agriculture, industry, energy, workforce mobility, human resource development, education, IT, media and climate change, among other areas”, the Foreign Office (FO) said. Both ministers emphasised the importance of strengthening people-to-people ties, facilitating workforce mobility, and promoting exchanges of business delegations from both countries to unlock new opportunities for trade, investment and institutional collaboration. FM Dar stressed the need for “timely implementation of agreed outcomes through close institutional coordination and sustained engagement between joint working group meetings”, the statement added. According to FO, the Oman FM thanked Pakistan for its warm hospitality, appreciated Pakistan’s efforts for regional peace and security, and reaffirmed Muscat’s commitment to further strengthening the longstanding partnership between the two countries. Dar commends Albusaidi’s efforts towards regional peace Speaking at the outset of the JMC session, Dar said the two had “worked out” certain areas of bilateral interest and discussed global issues in detail, including the US-Iran war, the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab and Gaza in their restricted meeting. Dar said the two sides had also discussed Jammu and Kashmir and other pressing regional issues. He commended Albusaidi’s leadership and efforts towards regional peace in the Middle East. “I personally greatly admire your efforts. I know how much hard work you have put in,” he said, noting that Pakistan’s position on the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) was “very unique”. “We are members of both the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) and, obviously, the United Nations and other multilateral bodies,” Dar said. He stressed, “There should not be any long gaps between bilateral engagements,” noting potential in the areas of trade, economic activities and investment opportunities. Dar said he had promised to visit Oman in 2027 to hold the next session of the commission there. He added that both sides had identified areas of mutual interest and discussed possible meetings. He said Pakistan and Oman cooperated closely and cordially, adding that although their diplomatic relations had completed 55 years, their ties went back “centuries”. Dar said the two countries shared a history of “love and affection”, particularly in relation to Balochistan and Gwadar. Referring to discussions on Bab al-Mandeb and recent developments involving the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, Dar said both sides shared similar views on resolving regional issues. He said the impact of regional tensions was also visible in Pakistan, where energy supply chains had been affected, and fuel prices had skyrocketed, adding that the “common man could not afford the resulting burden.” Speaking on the occasion, Albusaidi said Oman was committed to further strengthening bilateral engagement and cooperation in various fields that could bring greater benefits to the people of both countries. “I am delighted to be here with my delegation in Islamabad this morning, in this very warm, friendly and brotherly country, Pakistan, with which, as you have rightly said, we share bonds of history, culture, tradition and unity,” he said. He said the Pakistan-Oman JMC was one of the mechanisms for exploring further avenues of collaboration, adding that the two countries also had a business council and a political consultation mechanism between their foreign ministers. “We can do much more, and as we made a joint commitment this morning to make this meeting a success, I believe the more we do, the more we can deliver on the promise and the aspiration of our leaderships and our people,” Albusaidi said. He also commended Pakistan’s role in supporting dialogue and diplomacy in the region. “Your efforts to encourage engagement, understanding, respect and recognition are commendable, and I salute you for all your efforts,” he said, adding that Oman greatly appreciated Pakistan’s role in providing space for dialogue between Iran and the US. Albusaidi said there was significant potential for economic cooperation between Oman and Pakistan, particularly in trade, logistics, port connectivity, energy and food security. “The potential exists, and our task is to remove any obstacles and create the conditions that allow businesses to thrive so that we can fully benefit from this potential,” he said. He also called for greater cooperation in tourism, academic and technological fields, as well as more regular exchanges between the people of the two countries. “Once again, I appreciate the efforts of our private sector and industrial partners,” Albusaidi said, adding that he looked forward to further discussions on strengthening bilateral cooperation. Dar, Omani FM call for sustained bilateral engagement Earlier in the day, Dar also held a bilateral meeting with Albusaidi ahead of the JMC session, FO said. The visiting dignitary had arrived in Pakistan on Tuesday on a two-day visit. The two ministers reaffirmed the close, fraternal ties between Pakistan and Oman and underscored the importance of sustained high-level engagement to deepen cooperation in areas of mutual interest, particularly trade, investment and people-to-people contacts, according to FO. “The two sides also exchanged views on regional developments and emphasised the importance of dialogue and diplomacy in advancing lasting peace and stability,” FO said. Albusaidi commended Pakistan’s efforts to promote regional peace and security, while Dar acknowledged and appreciated Oman’s constructive role and shared aspirations for regional peace and stability, the statement added. A day earlier, FO said the JMC session would review the entire spectrum of Pakistan-Oman bilateral relations and strengthen cooperation. The visit “reflects the longstanding fraternal relations between Pakistan and Oman and is expected to further deepen mutually beneficial cooperation”. Last week, DPM Dar chaired an inter-ministerial meeting in Islamabad to review preparations for the upcoming JMC session, according to state-run Radio Pakistan. The meeting reviewed the agenda, bilateral agreements, and arrangements for the co-chairing of the JMC session, it said.

items.title: Lagos begins 35-day Lekki-Epe road repairs Thursday
items.description: Releases traffic advisory for motorists By Olasunkanmi Akoni LAGOS — The Lagos State Government will on Thursday commence a 35-day rehabilitation of damaged sections of the Eti-Osa-Lekki-Epe Expressway, covering Bonny Camp to Admiralty Way Junction and areas around Victoria Garden City (VGC). The government said traffic diversion arrangements would be introduced to minimise congestion and ensure the safety of road users during the rehabilitation. The Special Adviser to the Governor on Infrastructure, Olufemi Daramola, disclosed this on Wednesday during a stakeholders’ engagement organised by the Ministry of Works and Infrastructure to discuss the scope of work and traffic management plans. Daramola said the meeting was part of the government’s policy of consulting residents, businesses and road users before embarking on major infrastructure projects, adding that feedback from stakeholders would inform the implementation process. He appealed to residents and motorists to cooperate with the government during the exercise, particularly as Lagos prepares for increased traffic during the festive season. According to him, the rehabilitation is expected to improve road safety and ease movement along the strategic corridor, which connects residential communities, commercial centres and major industrial investments across the Lekki-Epe axis. The expressway provides access to the Lekki Free Zone, Dangote Refinery, Dangote Fertiliser Factory, Lekki Deep Sea Port and Eleganza Industrial Estate. It also serves major housing developments and educational institutions, including Pan-Atlantic University and Lagos Business School. However, rapid urbanisation, growing commercial activities and increasing traffic have accelerated the deterioration of some sections of the road. Daramola said the government was also addressing drainage concerns along the corridor, adding that the proposed Green Line rail project formed part of broader plans to improve transportation infrastructure in the area. He said the state had so far reconstructed and rehabilitated 69.44 kilometres of the expressway, comprising 49.7 kilometres of reinforced concrete pavement and 19.76 kilometres of flexible pavement. Residents raise concerns At the meeting, the Chairman of the Victoria Island and Ikoyi Residents Association, Prince Akin Fadoju, called for improved drainage infrastructure to address flooding in the area. Fadoju acknowledged that drainage problems predated the current administration but stressed the need for urgent intervention. Other stakeholders urged the government to ensure that traffic management officials were deployed throughout the construction period to direct motorists and prevent gridlock. They also called for the maintenance of alternative routes and adequate security for road users during the rehabilitation. The intervention is part of broader efforts to rehabilitate the Eti-Osa-Lekki-Epe Expressway. The government had earlier awarded the first phase, covering 18.75 kilometres from Eleko to Epe T-Junction in Ibeju-Lekki, in November 2020. The project was completed and commissioned in February 2023. Phases IIA and IIB, covering the stretch from Eleko Junction to Abraham Adesanya, were subsequently awarded, while rehabilitation works between Admiralty Intersection and Ajah Jubilee Flyover have also been completed. In April 2025, the government awarded early infrastructure development works for the proposed Green Line mass transit project. The proposed rail corridor will run from Marina through the Eti-Osa-Lekki-Epe axis towards the planned Lekki International Airport, connecting Lagos Island with the state’s rapidly developing eastern corridor. items.title: Sports Fund Administrator urges boxing fraternity to pursue partnerships beyond government funding
items.description: The Administrator of the Ghana Sports Fund, Dr David Kofi Wuaku, has urged boxing stakeholders to pursue stronger partnerships with corporate organisations and other institutions to address funding challenges confronting the sport. Dr Wuaku said sustainable sports development would require practical collaboration between the Fund, sporting associations, athletes and potential sponsors, particularly as sporting disciplines compete for limited financial resources. He made the call during a meeting with boxing representatives, who outlined difficulties in financing training, equipment and participation in international competitions. The representatives said financial constraints had affected their ability to participate in important competitions and appealed for assistance to support athletes seeking international exposure. Dr Wuaku acknowledged the concerns and encouraged the team to submit detailed proposals identifying its immediate needs and the expected benefits of proposed interventions. He said the Fund would consider practical programmes based on their merits, feasibility and likely impact, while also exploring opportunities to attract partners who could contribute to competitions, training and athlete development. The Administrator emphasised that the Fund could not necessarily meet every need presented by sporting associations. He therefore encouraged stakeholders to identify additional sources of support rather than depend exclusively on government financing. For boxing, potential areas for structured partnerships could include equipment provision, athlete preparation, competition sponsorship, coaching development and support for international participation. Such arrangements would require sporting associations to present credible programmes, define the support needed and demonstrate how sponsorship would contribute to measurable outcomes. Dr Wuaku also stressed the importance of accountability, saying the Fund would expect resources directed towards sports development to produce tangible benefits. The approach places responsibility on sports administrators to strengthen programme planning and establish credible relationships with prospective partners. For businesses, clearly defined programmes and transparent reporting could help provide a basis for assessing the value and impact of sports sponsorship. The meeting did not establish any confirmed sponsorship agreement or financial commitment. Instead, it highlighted the need for structured proposals and further engagement to identify practical opportunities for collaboration. Dr Wuaku reaffirmed the Fund’s willingness to work with the boxing fraternity and encouraged the representatives to develop proposals that could attract support and advance the development of the sport.

items.title: Pétrole : les cours repartent à la hausse face aux tensions au Moyen-Orient
items.description: Les cours du pétrole s'affichent un peu plus hauts mercredi, le marché continuant de s'inquiéter des hostilités entre les Houthis du Yémen et l'Arabie saoudite, ainsi que des risques dans le détroit d'Ormuz malgré la hausse récente des exportations en provenance du Golfe. Vers 10H15 GMT (12H15 à Paris), le prix du baril de Brent de la mer du Nord, pour livraison en décembre, prenait 0,77 % à 106,50 dollars. Son équivalent américain, le baril de West Texas Intermediate, pour livraison en novembre, gagnait 1,25 % à 95,32 dollars. « La reprise de l'approvisionnement en pétrole au Moyen-Orient était bien engagée en septembre, les exportations de brut des pays du Golfe se rapprochant des niveaux d'avant-guerre », indique l'Agence internationale de l'énergie (AIE), qui a publié mercredi son rapport mensuel sur le marché du pétrole. Mais « la récente intensification des attaques visant les infrastructures énergétiques régionales et le trafic de tankers menace de compromettre de nouveaux progrès », explique-t-elle. Les « opérations visant le cœur du territoire saoudien se poursuivront dans les jours à venir, ciblant les aéroports et les installations pétrolières de l'ennemi saoudien et les conséquences seront sévères », a notamment déclaré mercredi le porte-parole militaire des Houthis, Yahya Saree. Ces attaques « augmentent les risques pour les infrastructures pétrolières de l'Arabie saoudite et ses principaux oléoducs » et pour la capacité d'exportation de Ryad, souligne Arne Lohmann Rasmussen, analyste chez Global Risk Management. Par ailleurs, les incidents et attaques recensés par l'agence de sécurité maritime britannique UKMTO dans le détroit d'Ormuz se sont multipliés ces derniers jours. « L'Iran cherche délibérément à exercer une pression supplémentaire sur le marché pétrolier » pour mettre la pression sur Donald Trump, en particulier avant les élections législatives de mi-mandat aux Etats-Unis, selon M. Rasmussen. En raison de ces perturbations, même pour les navires qui circulent dans le Golfe, la logistique maritime est beaucoup plus complexe, le temps de transport plus long, et donc « les tarifs de transport du brut ont tellement augmenté qu'ils représentent désormais une part significative du coût » du baril, précisent les analystes de Morgan Stanley. The post Pétrole : les cours repartent à la hausse face aux tensions au Moyen-Orient appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .
